clinicalPearls: A usually benign fluid-filled cyst of the thymus, presenting in the anterior mediastinum or occasionally the neck
Congenital cysts arise from remnants of the thymopharyngeal duct, while acquired cysts follow inflammation, surgery, or radiotherapy
Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging performed for another reason
Cross-sectional imaging shows a well-defined, thin-walled, homogeneous fluid-density lesion without a solid enhancing component
A simple, uncomplicated cyst can often be managed conservatively with surveillance
Solid components, thick or irregular walls, or internal nodularity should raise concern for a cystic thymic neoplasm and prompt resection
Surgical excision is both diagnostic and curative when there is diagnostic uncertainty or symptomatic mass effect
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital thymic cysts develop from persistent epithelial remnants of the thymopharyngeal duct along the line of embryological thymic descent from the neck to the anterior mediastinum. Acquired cysts instead form through cystic degeneration provoked by inflammation, previous thoracic surgery or radiotherapy, or an adjacent neoplasm, and are often multilocular. In both cases the cyst is lined by thymic epithelium and filled with clear or proteinaceous fluid, and remains benign unless associated with an underlying tumour such as a thymoma or lymphoma undergoing cystic change.
additionalDifferentials: Bronchogenic or other foregut duplication cyst
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax to confirm fluid density and a thin wall
MRI to characterise cyst contents and exclude a solid component
Ultrasound for cervically extending or superficial lesions
Surgical excision with histology when the diagnosis is uncertain
PET-CT where a cystic neoplasm is suspected
redFlags: A solid, enhancing, or nodular component within the cyst
Thick, irregular walls or internal septation suggesting neoplasm
Associated lymphadenopathy raising concern for lymphoma
reference.prognosis: Simple thymic cysts are benign with an excellent prognosis, and complete excision of a symptomatic or indeterminate cyst is curative; the outlook depends on any underlying neoplasm if the cyst proves to be a cystic tumour.
pitfalls: Assuming every cystic anterior mediastinal lesion is a benign cyst and missing a cystic thymoma or lymphoma
Failing to characterise a solid component on adequate cross-sectional imaging
Aspirating a cyst without excluding malignancy when features are indeterminate
Overlooking that acquired cysts may accompany an adjacent tumour
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Manage a simple, thin-walled, uncomplicated cyst conservatively with periodic surveillance imaging
Undertake surgical excision with histology for symptomatic, enlarging or diagnostically indeterminate cysts
Resect promptly when solid components, thick or irregular walls or internal nodularity raise concern for a cystic thymoma or lymphoma
Characterise and follow lesions with contrast CT or MRI, adding PET-CT where a cystic neoplasm is suspected
Refer indeterminate anterior mediastinal lesions to thoracic surgery
Direct further management according to any underlying neoplasm if the cyst proves to be a cystic tumour
